entry.title: One YAML, Every Fine-Tune - Inside axolotl-ai-cloud/axolotl

link.title: One YAML, Every Fine-Tune - Inside axolotl-ai-cloud/axolotl

entry.content:
Fine-tuning an open model used to mean writing a training script: dataset glue, tokenizer surgery, trainer arguments, sharding flags, and a prayer that the checkpoint resumes. Axolotl replaces the script with a single YAML file and a codebase whose whole architecture exists to translate that YAML into a correct, memory-efficient training run. The result is one of the most widely used fine-tuning frameworks in the open-source world, and its source is a masterclass in how to layer configuration, data, and distributed training without letting any of them tangle. Version 0.21.1 under an Apache-2.0 license, it currently spans roughly 750 Python modules under its src tree, covering everything from classic Alpaca prompt formats to NVFP4 MoE LoRA kernels and asynchronous GRPO rollouts.

What makes the codebase worth reading is that it is honest about the messy parts. Every performance trick you have heard about - sample packing, flash attention swaps, FSDP2 with 4-bit bases, fused Liger kernels - lives here as an actual patch or plugin with clear seams, not as a blog diagram. You can trace one YAML key from the schema that validates it, through the loader that acts on it, to the trainer mixin that consumes it. As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

Overview: the CLI and config layer feeds dataset machinery and model loading; the trainer core consumes packed batches while patches and plugins reshape the model in between.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • cli/main.py is the dispatcher whose main at line 529 wires every subcommand from train to preprocess to merge to cloud launches.
  • utils/config/init.py at 636 lines reads the YAML, applies defaults and plugin additions, and hands it to validation.
  • utils/schemas/config.py defines AxolotlInputConfig at line 196, a 2240-line pydantic schema that is effectively the framework’s contract with users.
  • utils/data/sft.py starts at prepare_datasets line 49 and assembles raw, tokenized, and shuffled datasets for supervised runs.
  • prompt_strategies/chat_template.py implements ChatTemplateStrategy at line 308, turning chat rows into masked label tensors.
  • utils/samplers/multipack.py provides MultipackBatchSampler at line 252, the best-fit-decreasing bin packer that keeps sequences together.
  • loaders/model.py is ModelLoader at line 209, 1468 lines handling quantization configs, device maps, and attention impl selection.
  • train.py closes the loop with train at line 703: setup, execute, save, model card, plugin teardown.

Why You Need This

If you have read our tours of peft, accelerate, or deepspeed, you know the individual parts: adapters, sharding, ZeRO stages. Axolotl is the orchestration layer that binds them behind one config file, and reading it shows you what integration actually costs. The repo does not just call PEFT’s get_peft_model; it patches PEFT’s parameter wrappers, seeds adapter initialization deterministically, and validates that a saved adapter matches the patterns you asked for. Those are the failure modes you only discover after your third night-long run dies at step 4000.

It is also the best available map of the 2025-2026 fine-tuning frontier in executable form. QLoRA on FSDP2 without a full-precision replica per GPU, NVFP4 MoE adapters via custom Triton kernels, selective activation checkpointing with CPU offload, asynchronous GRPO with a rollout producer - each landed as a self-contained module you can read in isolation. When a technique confuses you in a paper, the odds are good this repo contains the production version of it. Our torchtitan tour showed a clean-room trainer; axolotl shows the same ideas bolted onto the Hugging Face ecosystem where most practitioners actually live.

Finally, the plugin architecture is a lesson in extension design. Liger kernels, the ScatterMoE LoRA library, evaluation hooks, and even cloud launchers all enter through the same BasePlugin contract, getting called at pre-config-load, pre-model-load, post-model-load, and post-train phases. Nothing core knows Liger exists; the patch manager just asks registered plugins to do their worst at defined moments. If you maintain any training tool and want to stop merging every user request into core, this is the pattern to steal.

Detailed view: entry and config, dataset machinery, model and adapter loading, the trainer core, RL and preference trainers, and the patch and kernel layer.

Start at the entry, because the config is the product. cli/train.py defines do_cli at line 88 and do_train at line 37; the config path lands in utils/config/init.py which merges plugin-added keys before utils/schemas/config.py validates against AxolotlInputConfig at line 196. The schema is worth an evening: every knob from sequence_len to flash_attention is declared with types and defaults, and a capability-aware subclass AxolotlConfigWCapabilities at line 1939 cross-references the declared attention implementation against the installed hardware before a single GPU is touched. When validation fails you get a pydantic error pointing at the exact key, not a CUDA OOM nine hours later.

The dataset machinery is the second act. utils/data/sft.py loads raw datasets at line 319, applies the selected strategy through prompt_strategies/chat_template.py whose ChatTemplateStrategy at line 308 builds input and label tensors from any Jinja chat template, and persists the tokenized result so runs after the first skip straight to loading at line 268. The strategy ABCs live in prompt_tokenizers.py with PromptTokenizingStrategy at line 43, and the legacy Alpaca family at line 162 shows how train-on-input masking works. For RL runs the parallel module utils/data/rl.py at 528 lines prepares preference and prompt datasets instead.

The packing story is where axolotl earns its throughput. utils/samplers/multipack.py implements MultipackBatchSampler at line 252: sequence lengths come in, ffd_check at line 33 validates the bin estimate, pack_group at line 69 does best-fit-decreasing, and generate_batches at line 378 emits index batches whose padding waste is reported by efficiency at line 597. The sampler plugs into AxolotlTrainer through _create_multipack_sampler at line 363 of core/trainers/base.py, and the matching collator V2BatchSamplerDataCollatorForSeq2Seq at line 213 of utils/collators/batching.py pads to the batch max rather than a global max. A monkeypatch teaches the stock HF Trainer about these variable-length batches so loss normalization counts real tokens, a detail that silently skews results if ignored.

Model loading is a 1468-line negotiation with reality. ModelLoader.load at line 313 of loaders/model.py runs pre-model-load patches, picks device map via _set_device_map_config at line 922, quantization via _set_quantization_config at line 1006, and attention via _set_attention_config at line 1105, then _build_model at line 1243 actually constructs the model and _build_adapters at line 727 attaches LoRA through loaders/adapter.py whose load_lora at line 414 and find_all_linear_names at line 60 decide what gets adapters. The deepest magic is monkeypatch/accelerate/fsdp2.py: fsdp2_load_full_state_dict at line 183 shards a full checkpoint across ranks while keeping 4-bit quantized parameters intact, fsdp2_prepare_model at line 583 applies activation checkpointing, and the QLoRA companion monkeypatch/fsdp2_qlora.py makes adapters trainable on the sharded quantized base - the CPU-staged loading that lets you fine-tune models bigger than any single GPU.

On top sit the trainers and plugins. AxolotlTrainer at line 114 of core/trainers/base.py overrides compute_loss at line 771 for proper token-level normalization and composes mixins from core/trainers/mixins/packing.py. RL lives in core/trainers/grpo/trainer.py with AxolotlGRPOTrainer at line 57 and a context-parallel variant at line 89 whose _generate_and_score_completions at line 297 does the rollout-scoring dance, while core/trainers/grpo/async_trainer.py builds a full producer-consumer system - AsyncDataProducer at line 368, RolloutDataset at line 529, AsyncGRPOTrainer at line 832 - so generation overlaps training. Plugins enter through integrations/base.py; LigerPlugin at line 34 of integrations/liger/plugin.py swaps fused kernels in pre_model_load at line 114, and KernelsPlugin at line 146 of integrations/kernels/plugin.py routes MoE adapters to the ScatterMoE library’s grouped kernels while registering house Triton ops like the swiglu in kernels/swiglu.py.

What happens after the last step matters just as much, and the post-training exit ramps are built in. train at line 703 of train.py finishes with save_trained_model at line 274, which handles the FSDP merge-and-rename path (a helper at line 252 renames merged shards to adapter form), writes the model card at line 488, and calls PluginManager.post_train so plugins can unload or upload. From there the CLI takes over: cli/merge_lora.py collapses adapters into base weights with a memory-efficient variant at line 119, and the export command drives utils/gguf.py whose export_gguf at line 149 resolves llama.cpp binaries, preflights the vocab and template at line 89, and quantizes straight to a deployable GGUF for llama.cpp or Ollama. A fine-tune that ends in a serving-ready file without leaving the tool is the actual deliverable most users want.

From Install to Fine-Tuned Model

The README’s uv-first install and one-command train:

curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
export UV_TORCH_BACKEND=cu130
uv venv --python 3.12
uv pip install torch==2.14.0 torchvision
uv pip install --no-build-isolation axolotl[deepspeed]
axolotl fetch examples
axolotl train examples/llama-3/lora-1b.yml

The same path programmatically, which is how notebooks and sweeps drive it:

from axolotl.cli.train import do_cli

do_cli(config="examples/llama-3/lora-1b.yml")

Change a few keys - base_model, learning_rate, lora_target_modules, flash_attention: true - and the identical command fine-tunes a different architecture; add rl: grpo with a reward function and the same entrypoint switches to the GRPO trainer.

Honest limits: axolotl’s breadth is also its surface area - the monkeypatch and model_support trees track upstream Hugging Face and torch releases closely, so pinning versions matters more here than in smaller tools. The config schema documents most keys, but exotic combinations (NVFP4 MoE plus context parallelism, say) carry caveats that only the docs’ support matrix admits to. And like every YAML-driven trainer, it will happily train a mediocre model on a mediocre dataset; no framework validates that your data was worth the GPU hours.
entry.summary: A source tour of axolotl, the configuration-driven fine-tuning framework: pydantic config validation, prompt strategies, multipack bin-packing, FSDP2 QLoRA patches, plugin integrations, and GRPO trainers.

entry.title: 100+ Models, One Command - Inside hiyouga/LLaMA-Factory
entry.content:
Where axolotl bets on one exhaustive YAML schema, LLaMA-Factory bets on breadth: one CLI that fine-tunes over a hundred model families, one data loader that speaks every open dataset format, and one stage dispatcher that walks from continuous pretraining through supervised fine-tuning into reward modeling, PPO, DPO, and KTO. The project behind the widely cited “Unified Efficient Fine-Tuning of 100+ Language Models” paper has become the default answer to “how do I fine-tune X” for a whole generation of practitioners, and it ships a Gradio web UI so the entire journey runs from a browser. Apache-2.0 licensed, it packs its power into a surprisingly compact src tree of about 180 Python files - most of the surface area lives in a handful of genuinely enormous modules.

Those big modules are the story. A 2686-line template file encodes every supported chat format as data; a 3502-line multimodal plugin file teaches every vision-language family how to emit training rows; a 978-line trainer utilities file carries the callbacks and metrics every stage shares. Reading the repo is really reading three or four epic files plus a lattice of small workflow scripts that glue them together. As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

Overview: the CLI routes to a stage dispatcher; argument parsing, the template registry, and dataset processing feed model loading and the workflows; a chat facade serves the result.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • cli.py is a 31-line console entry that forwards every subcommand to the launcher.
  • launcher.py at 185 lines routes train, chat, api, export, webui, and eval to their implementations.
  • hparams/parser.py defines get_train_args at line 395, fusing five argument families into one validated tuple.
  • train/tuner.py exposes run_exp at line 163 with the stage dispatch at line 69.
  • data/loader.py loads and merges datasets via get_dataset at line 276 with caching at line 229.
  • data/template.py is the template registry: register_template at line 681 defines every supported chat format.
  • data/processor/supervised.py tokenizes rows in SupervisedDatasetProcessor at line 51.
  • model/loader.py builds the model while chat/chat_model.py serves it afterwards.

Why You Need This

Every fine-tuning tool solves the same four problems - arguments, data, model prep, training loop - and comparing implementations is the fastest way to understand the trade space. Where the axolotl tour showed a pydantic schema validating one giant YAML, LLaMA-Factory shows the Hugging Face idiom: five dataclass families (model, data, training, finetuning, generating) parsed from CLI or dict and cross-verified in _verify_model_args at line 227 of the parser. Neither is wrong; seeing both teaches you what a config system must guarantee regardless of style. The same comparison holds for adapters - this repo’s model/adapter.py implements full, freeze, and LoRA tuning side by side, next to the PEFT internals we covered in the peft tour.

The template registry deserves particular attention because it quietly carries the entire “100+ models” claim. A chat model fine-tune is useless if the prompt format does not match the pretrained format, and this file turns that compatibility problem into data: each register_template call declares system messages, user and assistant wrappers, stop tokens, and tool-call encodings for one family. New model support lands as a few lines of registration rather than a fork of the trainer - which is exactly why the README’s day-0 support table keeps filling in. If you maintain any chat-adjacent system, this is the most complete public catalog of what varies between chat formats.

Multimodal support is the other eye-opener. The data/mm_plugin.py file gives every vision-language family - LLaVA, Gemma 3, InternVL, Kimi-VL and more - a plugin that converts raw rows into the exact interleave of text and image/video tokens that family’s model class expects, including pixel-value preprocessing and image token splicing. Rather than one generic VLM loader, the repo embraces per-family reality. And when the current architecture finally hits its limits, the v1 subtree shows the rewrite: a cleaner engine split (data_engine, model_engine, base_trainer) with its own plugin system - worth reading as a case study in how projects migrate themselves.

Detailed view: entry and dispatch, argument families, the data machinery with templates and multimodal plugins, model preparation, the six stage trainers, and the inference surface.

Follow one stage end to end. llamafactory-cli train lands in launcher.py, which calls run_exp at line 163 of train/tuner.py; read_args at line 112 of hparams/parser.py accepts either a dict or command-line tokens, and get_train_args at line 395 returns the five-class tuple after _verify_model_args at line 227 rejects contradictions like a missing template. The _training_function at line 69 then dispatches: stage sft goes to run_sft at line 41 of train/sft/workflow.py, while pt, rm, ppo, dpo, and kto each have a sibling workflow - and lines 92 through 136 show optional detours into hyper-parallel, Megatron-Bridge, and Megatron-core backends when those packages are installed.

The data path inside run_sft is the loader at work. data/loader.py merges every named dataset at line 164, converts rows via data/converter.py (alpaca, sharegpt, openai formats), resolves the chat template through get_template_and_fix_tokenizer at line 819 of data/template.py, and hands rows to the processors: SupervisedDatasetProcessor at line 51 of data/processor/supervised.py builds input_ids with labels masked outside responses, its packed subclass at line 146 concatenates sequences with position-id resets, and the PairwiseDatasetProcessor at line 30 of data/processor/pairwise.py produces the chosen/rejected pairs that DPO and reward stages consume. Collators from data/collator.py finish the batches.

Model preparation is the patcher’s show. model/loader.py picks quantization through model/model_utils/quantization.py - AQLM, AWQ, GPTQ, HQQ, EETQ, and bitsandbytes variants - then model/patcher.py applies patch_config at line 365 (rope scaling, attention impl, flash-attn selection), patch_model at line 437 (longlora shift attention, packed attention, MoE and vision fixes), and unsloth support from model/model_utils/unsloth.py when requested. init_adapter at line 317 of model/adapter.py then branches: full tuning at line 38, freeze tuning at line 57, and _setup_lora_tuning at line 147 covering LoRA, DoRA, PiSSA, and LoftQ variants. The workflow finishes by instantiating CustomSeq2SeqTrainer at line 47 of train/sft/trainer.py with metrics from train/trainer_utils.py.

The serving half closes the loop. ChatModel at line 39 of chat/chat_model.py wraps three engines - hf, vLLM (VllmEngine at line 46 of chat/vllm_engine.py), and sglang - behind one astream_chat interface; api/app.py exposes it as an OpenAI-compatible server; and the LLaMA Board web UI’s webui/runner.py submits training jobs straight into the same run_exp entry, so GUI and CLI are one system. Evaluation through eval/evaluator.py scores MMLU-style benchmarks with the same template machinery.

Two registries make the 100-model claim hold up. The template registry in data/template.py is a plain dict called TEMPLATES at line 678, filled by register_template at line 681 and consulted by get_template_and_fix_tokenizer at line 819; the base Template class at line 41 carries specializations like Llama2Template at line 454 for the older Llama chat format, and ReasoningTemplate at line 524 with its Qwen38ReasoningTemplate subclass at line 593 for models that emit thinking traces before answers. Multimodal support follows the same shape in mm_plugin.py, a 3,502-line module whose BasePlugin at line 421 defines the default vision interface and whose per-family subclasses - Gemma3Plugin at line 876, InternVLPlugin at line 1180, KimiVLPlugin at line 1330, and LlavaPlugin at line 1429 - override how images and videos expand into placeholder tokens, how processor outputs are cached, and how the collator stitches visual features into the sequence. Adding a new model family usually means registering one template and one plugin instead of touching the trainer at all.

The alignment stages get their own trainers with minimal duplication. CustomDPOTrainer at line 44 of train/dpo/trainer.py extends the TRL DPOTrainer and overrides concatenated_forward at line 219 to route preference batches through the repo’s own collators and mm plugin, while CustomPPOTrainer at line 64 of train/ppo/trainer.py inherits from both PPOTrainer and Trainer to blend rollout generation with the standard optimization step. Cross-cutting behavior lands in callbacks rather than trainer edits: LogCallback at line 174 of train/callbacks.py appends each stage’s timing and loss to the trainer_log.jsonl you find in every output directory, PissaConvertCallback at line 132 swaps PiSSA adapters between their init and training representations, ReporterCallback at line 433 writes the training report when a run ends, and ModuleProfilerCallback at line 491 measures per-module memory so you can spot which layers are worth offloading or quantizing. When one node is not enough, run_exp checks ray_args.use_ray and re-enters itself through Ray, with the placement-group helpers in trainer_utils.py - get_placement_group, get_ray_head_node_ip, sort_placement_group_by_node_ip - pinning workers across the cluster, so the same YAML scales from a single GPU to a multi-node job without edits.

From Install to Fine-Tuned Model

The README’s zero-code loop:

uv run llamafactory-cli webui
llamafactory-cli train examples/train_lora/qwen3_lora_sft.yaml
llamafactory-cli chat examples/inference/qwen3_lora_sft.yaml
llamafactory-cli export examples/merge_lora/qwen3_lora_sft.yaml

Or programmatically, one dict instead of YAML:

from llamafactory.train.tuner import run_exp

run_exp(args={
    "stage": "sft",
    "model_name_or_path": "Qwen/Qwen3-8B",
    "template": "qwen3",
    "dataset": "alpaca_en_demo",
    "finetuning_type": "lora",
    "output_dir": "qwen3-lora-out",
})

Swap stage to dpo with a pairwise dataset and the same entry runs preference tuning; point infer_backend at vllm and the same chat model serves hundreds of concurrent requests.

Honest limits: the breadth comes with weight - the giant template, mm_plugin, and trainer_utils files are dense and occasionally duplicate logic across stage trainers, so tracing one behavior can mean reading three files. The WebUI covers the happy path well but exotic combinations still want the CLI. And because so much support is template registration plus small patches, per-model quirks sometimes surface only in that model’s issue tracker, not the docs.
entry.summary: A source tour of LLaMA-Factory, the unified fine-tuning factory: a 2686-line chat template registry, multimodal plugins, stage dispatch from pretraining to PPO, and a v1 engine rewrite.

entry.title: Five Lines to Any Hardware - Inside huggingface/accelerate

link.title: Five Lines to Any Hardware - Inside huggingface/accelerate

entry.content:
Every PyTorch practitioner eventually hits the same wall: the training loop that ran beautifully on a laptop needs distributed ranks, gradient synchronization, loss scaling, and device juggling the moment it meets real hardware, and the boilerplate for all of that dwarfs the actual science. huggingface/accelerate, the Apache-2.0 library under most modern Hugging Face training stacks, takes a different path from the monolithic trainer frameworks: it refuses to own your loop. You keep writing the while-loop you already understand, add five lines, and the same script runs on one CPU, eight GPUs, a TPU pod, or any of a growing zoo of accelerators, with fp8, fp16, or bf16 mixed precision handled underneath. The library is deliberately thin in philosophy and decidedly not thin in engineering, which is exactly what makes its source worth reading. As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

The repository splits cleanly into four layers. The command-line layer gives you accelerate config, a questionnaire that saves your hardware setup, and accelerate launch, a 1338-line launcher that knows how to start single or multi-node runs without you memorizing torch.distributed.run flags. The state layer, state.py at 1181 lines, holds three singletons that discover the environment once and share it everywhere. The core layer is accelerator.py, 3738 lines around a single Accelerator class whose prepare method wraps whatever you hand it. And the device layer is a hook system: AlignDevicesHook and its offloading cousins move pieces of models between CPU, disk, and accelerator memory at execution time, the machinery that lets Transformers load a 30B model on a single consumer card. Reading the overview from left to right traces a request from the terminal, through environment detection, into the core, and down into the hooks that physically move tensors.

Overview of Accelerate: the CLI launches scripts that read shared state singletons, the Accelerator wraps training objects in one call, and the hook system performs device placement and offloading.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • accelerate config is a 70-line command that walks you through hardware questions and writes a reusable default_config.yaml.
  • accelerate launch is the 1338-line CLI that translates that config into worker processes, env vars, and backend-specific arguments.
  • launchers.py is the 285-line fallback that starts distributed runs from inside a plain script or notebook when no launcher process exists.
  • state.py is the source of truth: PartialState at line 123, AcceleratorState at 877, and GradientState at 1240 resolve the environment exactly once per process.
  • Accelerator is the class at line 184 that your script imports, holding prepare, backward, logging, and checkpoint methods.
  • prepare is the one call, at line 1414, that adapts a model, data loaders, optimizer, and scheduler to the current setup.
  • hooks.py is the placement engine, from the 58-line ModelHook base to AlignDevicesHook at line 242 and CpuOffload at 721.
  • big_modeling.py is the public toolkit for huge weights: init_empty_weights, cpu_offload, disk_offload, and dispatch_model.

Why You Need This

The README sells the library with a diff, and the diff is honest. You add the import, construct an Accelerator, replace the device literal with accelerator.device, wrap your model, optimizer, and dataloader in prepare, and swap loss.backward for accelerator.backward. Five edited lines. The same file then runs unchanged on a single GPU, a multi-GPU node, or a TPU, with mixed precision selected by config instead of code edits. A second variant in the README goes further: hand device placement to the library entirely and delete the to(device) calls, letting prepare move data and modules for you. This is a genuinely different contract from trainer frameworks; nothing is taken away, which is why so many projects adopt it incrementally rather than as a rewrite.

The hardware coverage in state.py is the part outsiders underestimate. The detection logic recognizes MULTI_GPU and XLA, of course, but also MULTI_MLU, MULTI_SDAA, MULTI_MUSA, MULTI_NPU, MULTI_HPU, MULTI_XPU, and MULTI_NEURON, falling back to MULTI_CPU or plain NO when nothing exotic is present. That list is the footprint of real-world inference and training hardware across vendors, and Accelerate is one of the few libraries that normalizes all of it behind one Accelerator object. Your loop never learns which accelerator it is on; the state singletons do, once, at import time, through a thread-local store that keeps parallel test runs from colliding.

The third reason is the big-model side, which has quietly become infrastructure for the entire ecosystem. init_empty_weights at line 62 of big_modeling.py builds a model on the meta device so a 70B parameter architecture costs kilobytes of RAM until weights arrive. dispatch_model at line 315 then assigns each layer to a device, and load_checkpoint_and_dispatch at line 524 streams the checkpoint in and wires it up. The CpuOffload hook, at line 721 of hooks.py, streams weights to the accelerator just before each forward and discards them after, trading a little latency for a lot of memory. If you have ever loaded a model larger than your GPU, you have run this code path.

Detail view: the launch commands, every major Accelerator method with its line number, the three state singletons and the device enum, the hook classes, and the big-model plus wrapper utilities.

The state layer rewards a close look because everything else leans on it. PartialState, at line 123 of state.py, is usable in any script with or without the Accelerator: it reads the environment variables that a launcher exported, queries the process group, and exposes device and distributed_type. AcceleratorState, at line 877, is the shared instance that all Accelerator objects in one process agree on, which is how a notebook can construct two Accelerators without starting two process groups. GradientState, at line 1240, is the smallest and most subtle: it tracks whether the current micro-batch is inside a no_sync window so that gradient accumulation skips process-group reductions on all but the last step. The AcceleratedOptimizer wrapper in optimizer.py, at line 38, consults that state before letting a step through, which is how accumulation works without touching your loop.

prepare itself is a dispatcher with seventeen special cases. The model path, prepare_model at line 1769, casts dtypes, attaches hooks, and handles compile and quantization integration; prepare_data_loader at line 2684 builds a DataLoaderShard whose BatchSamplerShard, at line 110 of data_loader.py, splits batches evenly and pads uneven tails so ranks never hang waiting for a straggler batch; prepare_optimizer and prepare_scheduler, at lines 2743 and 2787, wrap into the gated AcceleratedOptimizer and AcceleratedScheduler at line 25 of scheduler.py. The 1295-line data_loader.py module also contributes SeedableRandomSampler at line 73, which makes random data order reproducible across ranks, and DataLoaderDispatcher at line 726 for setups where the data loader lives on one process and steps happen elsewhere.

The backward path is where precision engineering hides. accelerator.backward at line 2828 routes through the native accelerator scaler for fp16, the native bf16 path, or fp8 handling depending on configuration, then calls the underlying loss.backward with the right arguments. clip_grad_norm_ at line 2988 knows to unscale gradients before measuring norms, a detail many hand-rolled loops get wrong. On the metrics side, gather_for_metrics at line 3108 collects tensors from every rank and drops the padding that the even-batch sharding introduced, so your accuracy numbers are computed on real samples only. save_state at line 3624 and load_state at 3790 round-trip the entire setup, model, optimizer, schedulers, random states, and registration order included, which is what makes interrupted distributed runs resumable at all.

The hook system is the architectural trick that keeps all of this composable. ModelHook at line 58 of hooks.py is a tiny class that wraps a module’s forward and detach; add_hook_to_module at line 147 attaches one to any nn.Module by overriding its forward, and SequentialHook at 116 chains them. AlignDevicesHook at line 242 is the workhorse: on entry it casts and moves a module’s parameters and buffers to its execution device, runs the wrapped forward, and optionally offloads again on exit. attach_align_device_hook_on_blocks at line 587 applies it recursively to every block of a model, which is precisely how dispatch_model implements its device map. The 742-line big_modeling.py module is just the public face of this machinery, and utils/modeling.py, at 1942 lines, supplies the weight-loading and offload-store utilities underneath, while utils/operations.py, at 808 lines, converts tensor sends, pads, and reductions into their distributed equivalents.

From Install to a Launched Run

Configure once, then launch:

pip install accelerate

accelerate config          # answer questions about GPU count, precision, distributed setup
accelerate launch train.py # starts single or multi-GPU training with zero code flags

Inside train.py, the whole integration is the five-line diff from the README:

# from accelerate import Accelerator
# accelerator = Accelerator()
# device = accelerator.device
# model, optimizer, data = accelerator.prepare(model, optimizer, data)
# accelerator.backward(loss)

The first two commands pick up default_config.yaml written by the questionnaire, so teammates and CI machines share one launch recipe instead of a wiki page of torchrun flags.

Honest limits: Accelerate deliberately does not schedule training for you, so learning-rate policy, evaluation cadence, and checkpoint rotation remain your loop’s job, and projects that want those managed graduate to Trainer or TRL on top. The five-line promise holds for standard loops, but exotic patterns such as two optimizers with different accumulation schedules or hand-written process-group collectives still leak distributed concepts through the abstraction. The hook-based offloading trades latency for memory and is tuned for inference-shaped workloads, not every training shape. And the device zoo, impressive as the enum is, means the long tail of accelerators gets community-tested coverage rather than vendor-certified support. What the source shows, line after line, is an unusual discipline: a library that grew to underpin an ecosystem while refusing to take your training loop hostage.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of huggingface/accelerate: how one 3738-line Accelerator class, three state singletons, and a hook system for device placement turn a raw PyTorch training loop into multi-GPU, TPU, and mixed-precision code.

entry.title: From Float32 to Four Bits - Inside pytorch/ao

link.title: From Float32 to Four Bits - Inside pytorch/ao

entry.content:
Quantization libraries have a reputation for being bolt-on afterthoughts: a separate graph mode, a foreign config format, kernels that break the moment you wrap your model in torch.compile. TorchAO, launched by the PyTorch team in September 2024 and versioned 0.19.0 in this tree, takes the opposite approach. It is pure native PyTorch, BSD 3-Clause licensed, and it works out of the box with torch.compile and FSDP2 across most HuggingFace models. The numbers on its README are the reason it ended up as the default quantization backend for HuggingFace Transformers, vLLM, ExecuTorch, and diffusers: Llama-3.1-70B pre-training runs 1.5x faster with float8 training, QAT recovers 67 percent of quantized accuracy degradation on Gemma3-4B, and an int4-quantized Llama-3-8B serves 1.89x faster inference with 58 percent less memory. As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

The design idea that holds the whole repository together is a two-layer split. The top layer is a small grammar of configs: dataclasses like Int4WeightOnlyConfig or Float8DynamicActivationFloat8WeightConfig that describe what you want, not how to do it. The bottom layer is a family of torch.Tensor subclasses, each of which owns its own quantize, dequantize, and matmul dispatch. Between them sits a registry that maps every config type to a function that walks the model and swaps linear weights in place. Everything else, from quantization-aware training to low-bit optimizers to experimental MoE kernels, plugs into that same registry pattern. Reading the overview from left to right traces one linear layer from a config object to a packed four-bit tensor running custom kernels.

Overview of TorchAO: quantize_ consumes AOBaseConfig subclasses with granularity choices, dispatches through the transform registry to tensor subclasses for int4, NF4, and float8, while QAT and float8 training flows and low-bit optimizers feed native C++ and CUDA ops.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • quantize_ is the public entry point at line 299 of an 1817-line quant_api.py that also hosts every inference config dataclass.
  • AOBaseConfig at line 27 of a 329-line core module is the abstract parent all workflow configs extend, defining layout and filter hooks.
  • The transform registry is a 52-line module holding the handler dict at line 13, with register_quantize_module_handler at 19 letting any package plug in.
  • TorchAOBaseTensor at line 721 of 1272-line utils.py is the subclass contract every quantized tensor implements.
  • Int4Tensor at line 57 of 627 lines stores packed four-bit weights, with packing variants like tile_packed_to_4d in a 391-line sibling file.
  • Float8Tensor at line 84 of 1126 lines carries float8 data plus scales for dynamic float8 inference.
  • QATConfig at line 43 of 481 lines drives quantization-aware training through a prepare step and a convert step.
  • The low-bit optimizers live in a 430-line file: AdamW8bit at 309, AdamW4bit at 342, AdamWFp8 at 375, all sharing _AdamBase at 19.

Why You Need This

If you serve large language models, memory bandwidth is your tax bracket. A 70-billion-parameter model in bfloat16 needs about 140 gigabytes just for weights, which means multiple accelerators before you serve a single token. TorchAO’s int4 weight-only path compresses those weights to roughly a quarter of the size while keeping the compute in higher precision, and the measured results are concrete: 1.73x speedup with 65 percent less memory for Gemma3-12b-it on an H100, 1.5 to 1.6x on gemma-3-27b-it with float8 dynamic quantization, and 1.54x and 1.27x on Flux.1-Dev and CogVideoX-5b image and video generation respectively. On the mobile side, a Qwen3-4B model quantized to int8 activations with int4 weights runs at 14.8 tokens per second in 3379 megabytes on an iPhone 15 Pro through ExecuTorch.

If you train models, the float8 story matters even more. The float8 data type halves the bytes per element of bfloat16, but naive casting wrecks convergence because float8 has almost no mantissa bits near zero. TorchAO’s training stack handles amax history, per-tensor or per-row scaling, and delayed scaling so that Llama-scale pre-training runs at 1.43 to 1.51x on 70B and 405B models with FSDP2, and rowwise float8 yielded 1.34 to 1.43x at 2k H100 GPU scale with matching loss curves. The newest prototype pushes the same idea to mixture-of-experts: MXFP8 grouped matmuls measured roughly 1.45x on the MoE layer of Llama4 Scout and about 1.25x on DeepSeekV3 671B, with a 1.28x end-to-end result on a Crusoe B200 cluster.

If you do both, the QAT loop is the piece most libraries get wrong. Post-training quantization is cheap but costs accuracy; quantization-aware training recovers it, but many implementations are fragile under torch.compile. TorchAO’s QAT recovered up to 96 percent of the accuracy degradation on Llama-3-8B, 67 percent on Gemma3-4B, and the approach has since been adopted by Unsloth and Axolotl for fine-tuning workflows. Because everything composes with torch.compile and FSDP2, you can float8-train, QAT-finetune, int4-quantize, and serve through vLLM without leaving the PyTorch ecosystem. The January 2025 integration with GemLite and SGLang measured 1.1 to 2x faster inference across batch sizes and tensor parallel widths.

Detail view of TorchAO: config dataclasses extend AOBaseConfig with granularity, the engine walks modules through the handler registry, workflow folders build Int4, Int8, NF4, and Float8 tensors on quant_primitives, the float8 training stack swaps in Float8Linear, and optimizers plus custom ops round out the runtime.

The engine mechanics are worth reading because they are small. quantize_ at line 299 accepts either a plain AOBaseConfig or an FqnToConfig mapping that targets specific fully-qualified module names, checked from line 336 onward. For a plain config it looks up the handler by type in the registry dict at line 359, then calls _replace_with_custom_fn_if_matches_filter at line 122, which recurses named_modules and replaces each matching linear in place, optionally moving modules to a device first so quantization runs faster. The registry itself, declared at line 13 of the 52-line transform_module.py, is populated by register_quantize_module_handler at line 19. Prototype packages reuse the same mechanism: SmoothQuant’s api registers against the handler dict at line 151 of its module, and AWQ does the same from its core file, which is why experimental flows feel identical to stable ones.

The tensor layer is where the numerics live. quant_primitives.py, at 2388 lines, implements the reference math: quantize_affine at line 364 plus choose_qparams and dequantize primitives that do scaled integer arithmetic on plain tensors. Each subclass then specializes dispatch. Int4Tensor at line 57 comes in packing flavors, tile_packed_to_4d in a 391-line file that reshapes packed weights into four dimensions so torch.compile fuses the matmul, and a preshuffled layout matching cuBLASLt operand order. NF4Tensor at line 580 of a 1221-line file is the QLoRA substrate: to_nf4 at line 1077 builds it with 64-wide quantization blocks and 256-wide scaler blocks, and the normal-float lookup table keeps gradient flow intact for adapter training. Float8Tensor at line 84 handles the inference side, including a scaled conv3d dispatch at line 528.

The float8 training stack is a separate, older flow that predates the config registry. Its config module is 381 lines, defining the ScalingType enum at 19, Float8LinearRecipeName at 141, and Float8LinearConfig at 180, which records per-operand cast and scaling choices. convert_to_float8_training at line 86 of a 215-line utils file walks the model and swaps every nn.Linear for Float8Linear, defined at line 206, which tracks amax history and applies delayed scaling; the Float8TrainingTensor at line 240 of 376 lines carries data plus amax so FSDP2 can shard it, and float8_ops.py provides 605 lines of casting and scaled_mm helpers. This is the flow TorchTitan uses for its float8 pre-training recipes. Alongside it, the MoE prototype pairs a 1088-line mxfp8_grouped_mm.py with a 252-line config, expert-parallel dispatch and combine modules under its ep folder, and CuteDSL kernels for fused quantization.

The remaining corners round out the lifecycle. The optim package keeps optimizer states small: the 430-line adam.py implements AdamW8bit, AdamW4bit, and AdamWFp8 on one base class at line 19, shrinking state memory by 2 to 4x with only a few hundred lines of code, while CPUOffloadOptimizer at line 18 of a 180-line file pins parameters and states in CPU memory and runs fused steps there, cutting GPU VRAM by around 60 percent in the README’s example. Sparsity has a native path: ops.py, at 409 lines, registers torch.ops.torchao kernels including to_sparse_semi_structured_cutlass_sm9x_f8 at line 198, backed by CUDA sources under torchao/csrc for 2:4 semi-structured masks that gave 1.1x inference and 1.3x training speedups on SAM and ViT. And QAT’s internals are a three-file story: FakeQuantizeConfig at line 413 of fake_quantize_config.py, a 477-line fake_quantizer.py with learnable-scale variants, and a 653-line qat linear swap-in, coordinated by a 28-line two-step module that wires prepare before training and convert after.

From Install to Quantized Inference

Install the stable wheel, optionally adding the MSLK kernel package for float8 and nvfp4 inference kernels:

pip install torchao
# optional accelerated kernels
pip install mslk --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu130

Quantize a loaded model to int4 with the tile-packed layout and the HQQ qparams algorithm, then load a float8 rowwise model through HuggingFace Transformers:

import torch
from transformers import TorchAoConfig, AutoModelForCausalLM
from torchao.quantization import (
    Int4WeightOnlyConfig,
    Float8DynamicActivationFloat8WeightConfig,
    PerRow,
    quantize_,
)

# int4 weight-only, packed for torch.compile
quantize_(model, Int4WeightOnlyConfig(group_size=32,
    int4_packing_format="tile_packed_to_4d",
    int4_choose_qparams_algorithm="hqq"))

# or load pre-quantized float8 rowwise from the Hub
config = TorchAoConfig(quant_type=Float8DynamicActivationFloat8WeightConfig(granularity=PerRow()))
fp8_model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    "Qwen/Qwen3-32B", dtype="auto", device_map="auto",
    quantization_config=config)

For serving, the Hub-hosted pytorch/Qwen3-32B-FP8 checkpoint runs directly under vLLM with the torchao backend enabled. For training-side use, convert_to_float8_training swaps linears before you wrap the model in FSDP2, and the QAT flow wraps any base config: pass QATConfig with a step flag of prepare to insert fake quantizers, train normally, then convert to produce the final quantized model.

Honest limits: the int4 and int8 inference kernels are tuned for linear layers on recent NVIDIA hardware, so exotic architectures, CPU-only serving, or non-linear-heavy models see smaller gains, and the ARM low-bit kernels target a narrower op set. The float8 training flow assumes accelerator support for float8 matmuls and interacts delicately with gradient accumulation and distributed setups, which is why the docs carry a compatibility table for torch and CUDA versions. MoE MXFP8 training is explicitly a prototype under torchao/prototype, and sparsity paths depend on specific tensor-core generations. None of that dims the core achievement: a quantization stack where every workflow is a config object, every quantized tensor is an honest torch.Tensor, and the whole thing compiles.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of pytorch/ao: how quantize_ and AOBaseConfig swap linear weights for Int4, NF4, and Float8 tensor subclasses, with QAT prepare and convert steps, float8 training recipes, and low-bit optimizers.

entry.title: One Booster, Every Parallelism - Inside hpcaitech/ColossalAI

link.title: One Booster, Every Parallelism - Inside hpcaitech/ColossalAI

entry.content:
Training a modern large model is a combinatorics problem disguised as a systems problem: data parallel or tensor parallel or stage parallel, optimizer states on GPU or CPU, activations recomputed or offloaded, and every combination trades memory against throughput differently. hpcaitech/ColossalAI, the Apache-2.0 project from HPC-AI Technology, is one of the most complete open answers: a single training facade called Booster, behind which a family of plugins can turn on any mix of data, tensor, and stage parallelism, ZeRO-style optimizer sharding, chunk-based CPU offloading, FP8 mixed precision, and mixture-of-experts, all without rewriting the model. The project’s own README benchmark is aggressive about it: a 70B Llama-like model at 811.79 TFLOPS per GPU on 16 H200s with a hybrid layout, and B200 nodes beating H200 by 50 to 70 percent on throughput. As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

The architecture is a stack of increasingly clever wrappers. At the top sits Booster, a facade class whose boost method accepts any model, optimizer, and plugin and returns wrapped versions that behave like the originals. Plugins decide everything: the flagship HybridParallelPlugin composes data, tensor, and stage parallelism with three optimizer tiers, while GeminiPlugin brings the chunked memory system that migrates parameters between GPU and CPU in large blocks. Underneath, the Shardformer rewrites transformer architectures module by module for tensor parallel execution, guided by per-model policy files, and the DTensor layout engine supplies the distributed math. Around the core live an inference system with its own KV cache and server, Triton kernels for attention primitives, and MoE operations. Reading the overview from left to right follows one training step from the facade, through plugin selection, into the memory and sharding machinery.

Overview of ColossalAI: the Booster facade delegates to a plugin family, Gemini chunks migrate parameter memory, and the Shardformer plus DTensor engine handles tensor-parallel surgery.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Booster is the facade at line 33: boost, backward, no_sync, LoRA helpers, and model, optimizer, and scheduler save and load all route through it.
  • colossalai.initialize is the 157-line boot sequence that builds the parallel context from launcher environment variables.
  • Plugin is the 74-line contract every parallel strategy implements, deciding how models, optimizers, and dataloaders get wrapped.
  • HybridParallelPlugin is the flagship at line 929, composing data, tensor, and stage parallelism with naive, AMP, and ZeRO optimizer tiers.
  • GeminiDDP is the 875-line memory wrapper that keeps parameters in chunks which migrate on demand.
  • ChunkManager plus chunk.py pack parameters and optimizer states into large, pinned, movable memory blocks.
  • LowLevelZeroOptimizer partitions gradients and optimizer states across the data-parallel group, ZeRO stage 1 and 2 style.
  • Shardformer is the 43-line engine that, given a policy file such as the 487-line LlamaPolicy, splits a transformer for tensor parallel training.

Why You Need This

The benchmark table in the README is the honest sales pitch, and it is worth reading closely. On 8 H200 GPUs training a 7B Llama-like model with ZeRO-2 data parallelism, Colossal-AI reports 17.13 samples per second at 534.18 TFLOPS per GPU. Switch to a 70B model on 16 H200s with the same ZeRO setup and it holds 3.27 samples per second at 469.1 TFLOPS. The hybrid layouts are where it gets interesting: zero1 plus tensor-parallel-2 plus 4-way stage splitting reaches 805.69 TFLOPS per GPU on 8 B200s for the 7B model and 811.79 on 16 H200s for the 70B, with peak memory around 100GB per card. The project’s headline numbers, 50 percent higher throughput for the 7B and over 70 percent for the 70B when moving to B200, are all measured with these in-repo configurations, and the benchmark scripts sit in the examples tree for verification.

The second reason is architectural: Booster is one of the cleanest plugin systems in the training-framework space. The facade at line 33 of booster.py exposes about thirty public methods, from boost at line 126 through backward at 175, load_model at 291, save_model at 315, optimizer save and load at 352 and 372, and LoRA helpers enable_lora at 240 and save_lora_as_pretrained at 418. Every one of those delegates to the active plugin, which means the difference between pure data parallel, FSDP, ZeRO, Gemini offloading, or full 3D parallelism is a config object, not a code change. A 44-line accelerator shim abstracts the hardware calls underneath, and the 157-line initialize module wires the parallel context from the launcher environment before any of it runs.

The third reason is the memory science. Gemini, the chunked memory system, is Colossal-AI’s answer to the question of what to do when parameters, gradients, and optimizer states do not fit: pack them into large chunks rather than moving tensors one by one. chunk.py, at 560 lines, implements a chunk as a contiguous memory region with a GPU window and a pinned CPU shard, and manager.py, at 270 lines, allocates and tracks them. A placement policy module, 240 lines, decides what lives where, and gemini_hook.py moves data at the four boundaries of a training step: before and after forward, before and after backward. The companion LowLevelZeroOptimizer partitions gradients through a bookkeeping layer of bucket and gradient stores, so stage 1 and 2 sharding work with asynchronous reduction hooks. Reading these files is a graduate course in memory management.

Detail view: the Booster facade and its entry methods, the full plugin family, the Gemini chunk machinery from manager to hooks, the Shardformer stack, and the MoE, FP8, and kernel support layer.

The HybridParallelPlugin file is where the composition happens, and its class layout tells the story. HybridParallelModule, at line 60 of hybrid_parallel_plugin.py, is the model wrapper that knows about tensor-parallel groups and stage boundaries; HybridParallelNaiveOptimizer at line 279 is the plain data-parallel path; HybridParallelAMPOptimizer at line 491 adds fp16 and bf16 loss scaling; and HybridParallelZeroOptimizer at line 667 extends the LowLevelZeroOptimizer so that ZeRO sharding works on top of the other two parallel axes simultaneously. The plugin itself, at line 929, extends the stage-parallel plugin base, which is why the same config can express the zero1-plus-TP2-plus-4-way-stage layout from the benchmark table. A separate MoE hybrid variant exists for expert models, and there are baseline torch DDP and FSDP plugins for apples-to-apples comparisons. The facade covers the interaction patterns a multi-axis run actually needs: Booster.no_sync at line 223 creates accumulation windows where gradients skip cross-rank reduction, and the scheduler save and load methods at lines 400 and 409 round-trip learning-rate state alongside the optimizer, so a resumed 3D run restarts warm rather than cold.

The project’s ecosystem is evidence the abstraction survives contact with real workloads. Open-Sora, the team’s video-generation effort, trains its diffusion transformers on this stack; ColossalChat used it for the full RLHF sequence on chat models; Colossal-LLaMA-2 demonstrated domain-specific fine-tuning in a half-day of training on rented hardware; and a February 2025 guide walked through fine-tuning DeepSeek’s 671B-parameter model with the upgraded toolchain. Those projects exercise very different corners of the plugin matrix, video generation favoring activation-heavy stage splits, RLHF favoring the inference side, and 671B-scale tuning leaning entirely on the chunked memory system. A library that hosts all four under one facade has put its abstraction where the workloads are.

The Shardformer is the component outsiders should study first, because tensor parallelism is usually the most painful part to implement by hand. The engine, shardformer.py, is only 43 lines: it takes a model, a ShardConfig of 110 lines of flags, and a policy, then performs the module surgery. The policies folder holds one file per architecture, and LlamaPolicy at 487 lines shows the pattern: each attention, MLP, and normalization sublayer is annotated with the sharding spec it should receive, plus optimizations like fused kernels where the groups allow. The DTensor engine underneath, in the d_tensor package with api, comm_spec, sharding_spec, and layout_converter modules, computes and converts the distributed layouts so that a matrix split four ways reduces correctly. Getting this wrong produces silent divergence; the policy files are effectively reviewed recipes.

The support layer rounds out the picture. The quantization package ships fp8.py and fp8_hook.py, the one-line FP8 mixed-precision integration the project blog credits with cutting training cost by up to 30 percent, plus bitsandbytes integration in bnb.py. The kernel package holds Triton implementations of the primitives large models need, from rms_layernorm and fused rotary embeddings to flash decoding and KV cache copy routines. The inference package is a serving system of its own, with core, executor, kv_cache, and server subpackages, and the auto_parallel module carries the compiler side: passes, checkpoint planning, offload planning, and profilers that reason about sharding choices before you commit them. The mixture-of-experts support lives in a compact _operation module plus its plugin variant, enough to see how experts are dispatched across ranks.

From Install to a Launched Run

The Llama example’s Gemini benchmark script shows the launcher in real form:

pip install colossalai
git clone https://github.com/hpcaitech/ColossalAI
cd ColossalAI/examples/language/llama

# one command starts 8 workers and applies the Gemini chunked-memory config
colossalai run --nproc_per_node 8 --hostfile hosts.txt benchmark.py -g -x -b 16

Inside the training script, the only structural change is the Booster pattern: construct a plugin, call booster.boost(model, optimizer), and train through booster.backward instead of loss.backward. Everything else, from chunk migration to gradient bucketing, happens inside the wrappers.

Honest limits: Colossal-AI’s breadth is also its operating cost. The plugin matrix multiplies, and exotic combinations such as MoE plus stage parallelism plus FP8 carry compatibility caveats that only the test suite fully maps. The custom kernels and CUDA extensions mean installation is heavier than a pure-Python library, with build toolchains that matter on older driver stacks. The headline benchmark numbers come from the project’s own hardware and scripts; reproducing 800-plus TFLOPS per GPU requires the exact H200 or B200 configurations listed. And the Gemini chunk system, while elegant, tunes through several interacting knobs, chunk size and placement policy chief among them, that reward experimentation. What the source demonstrates is a serious systems argument: parallelism strategies are composable objects, and a good facade makes the combinatorics navigable.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of hpcaitech/ColossalAI: how the Booster facade, a plugin family spanning 3D parallelism and ZeRO, chunk-based Gemini memory, and the Shardformer make large model training fit on the hardware you have.

entry.title: The Runtime That Made Serving Transformers Cheap - Inside OpenNMT/CTranslate2

link.title: The Runtime That Made Serving Transformers Cheap - Inside OpenNMT/CTranslate2

entry.content:
When translation or speech-recognition servers needed to handle real traffic on real hardware, the OpenNMT ecosystem discovered that general deep learning frameworks were the wrong tool: too much memory, too much overhead, too little control over precision. The answer is CTranslate2, a C++ and Python library for efficient inference with Transformer models, MIT-licensed and maintained by SYSTRAN with the OpenNMT community since 2018. Its README is refreshingly concrete: a custom runtime applying weights quantization, layers fusion, batch reordering, and padding removal, with benchmark tables showing a base Transformer going from 209 tokens per second under TensorFlow to 1126 with int8 and vocabulary mapping on the same four CPU threads, and GPU numbers that traded blows with FasterTransformer. The model zoo it covers has grown far beyond translation: Whisper, T5, Llama, Mistral, Gemma, Qwen2, BLOOM, BERT, and wav2vec2 all run in this one custom engine. As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

The tree is small compared with the frameworks it replaces, and that is the point: few dependencies, a deliberate per-device op pattern, and a serialization format designed around quantization from day one. Python converters turn checkpoints from Hugging Face Transformers, OpenNMT-py, OpenNMT-tf, Fairseq, Marian, and OPUS-MT into that format, the C++ runtime loads it onto CPU or GPU, and identical op names dispatch to hand-written paths per architecture. Reading the overview from left to right follows one converted checkpoint from disk to a parallel replica pool, through beam search decoding, into ISA-templated CPU kernels or vendored GPU attention.

Overview of CTranslate2: converters write the optimized model format, the model zoo builds layers per architecture, replica pools run beam or greedy decoding, ops dispatch per device to ISA-templated CPU kernels or the CUDA runtime with vendored FlashAttention-2 and AWQ int4, and pybind wrappers plus a CLI expose it all.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • transformers.py is the 4324-line Hugging Face converter, one of seven converter modules wired into console scripts by setup.py, including ct2-transformers-converter.
  • model.cc at 925 lines loads the format: Model::load at 553 and ModelLoader::load at 851, over get_variable at 245 and the 514-line storage_view.cc tensor container.
  • whisper.cc at 865 lines implements the speech model: encode at 80, generate at 122 and 233, token-level align at 425 over dtw.cc, and language detection at 585.
  • replica_pool.h is the 384-line scheduling heart, with thread_pool.cc at 186 and batch_reader.cc at 229 feeding one model replica per worker.
  • decoding.cc at 1382 lines holds the strategies: BiasedDecoder at 256 for constrained prefixes, BeamSearch::search at 425, and GreedySearch::search at 733.
  • transformer.cc at 902 lines builds the layers, with encoder and decoder layer classes at 54 and 150 and the attention layer at 112 of attention_layer.cc.
  • backend.cc at 141 lines selects among MKL, oneDNN, Apple Accelerate, OpenBLAS, and Ruy at runtime while cpu_isa.cc picks AVX2, AVX512, or NEON.
  • kernels.cc at 759 lines is the int8 story: quantize_s8 at 640 and dequantize_gemm_output at 725, fusing gelu, swish, and tanh into the dequantization epilogue.

Why You Need This

The first reason is the economics of serving. The README benchmark is not marketing fluff because the scripts live in tools/benchmark: a 5x CPU speedup over TensorFlow with a quarter of the memory, achieved by techniques this codebase makes legible. Layers fuse, padding disappears, batches reorder by length, quantization shrinks weights to a quarter on disk, and caching allocators on both CPU and GPU adapt memory to request size. For anyone running Whisper transcriptions, machine translation endpoints, or LLM generation on constrained hardware, CTranslate2 remains one of the most efficient paths in open source, and because the project promises backward compatibility for production users, the optimizations arrive without breaking your deployment. The same discipline explains its longevity in production stacks that predate the LLM boom.

The second reason is that the precision ladder is implemented end to end rather than delegated. The README lists FP16, BF16, INT16, INT8, and AWQ INT4, and the tree shows all five: quantize and dequantize ops exist as per-device dispatch pairs, the CPU int8 path quantizes activations per row in quantize_s8 at line 640 of kernels.cc and folds activation functions into dequantize_gemm_output at 725, and the AWQ folder implements 4-bit GEMV and GEMM with gemv_gpu.cu at 548 lines and gemm_gpu.cu at 543. On the GPU side the runtime even vendors FlashAttention-2, thirty-two sm80 instantiation files covering head dimensions 32 through 256 in fp16 and bf16 including split-KV variants for long contexts, reachable through the 175-line flash attention layer. If you read the quantization tour of pytorch/ao earlier in this series, this repository is the serving-side mirror: the same ideas, engineered for a custom runtime instead of PyTorch.

The third reason is the CPU engineering, which most inference projects neglect. backend.cc carries a GemmBackend enum across MKL, oneDNN, Accelerate, OpenBLAS, and Ruy with a CT2_USE_MKL environment override at line 11, and one binary can ship several backends and instruction sets, selected at runtime from CPU information as the README says, with cpu_isa.cc offering explicit overrides for AVX2, AVX512, and NEON at lines 48 through 56. The kernels themselves are templated on the ISA through vec.h, vec_avx.h, vec_avx512.h, and vec_neon.h, so the same C++ source compiles into dispatch targets for x86-64 and AArch64. Add the vocabulary map, which restricts output softmax to source-dependent candidates via get_candidates at line 53 of vocabulary_map.cc, and the int8-plus-vmap benchmark row starts to look earned rather than lucky.

Detail view: model_reader and storage_view carry the format, the model factory builds language, Whisper, and wav2vec2 replicas, decoding strategies step decoder layers through attention and GEMM ops, CPU backends and ISA templates or CUDA allocators with AWQ and FlashAttention kernels execute them, and the Python converters and specs define what the format holds.

The runtime core is a study in restraint. include/ctranslate2 exposes a small API surface: Translator and Generator over replica_pool.h, batch readers for streaming inputs, and StorageView as the universal tensor. src/translator.cc at 194 lines submits jobs, translate_batch_async at 8 returning futures while translate_batch at 46 blocks, with scoring and text-file helpers behind them. The pool template in replica_pool.h pairs one model replica per worker thread, so multiple batches run in parallel and asynchronously across GPUs or CPU cores, exactly the concurrency the README promises. Decoding then runs in decoding.cc: beam expansion and reranking in BeamSearch::search at 425, sampling with the multinomial, gumbel_max, and topp_mask ops in GreedySearch::search at 733, and BiasedDecoder at 256 enabling the interactive decoding features, like autocompleting a partial sequence, that the documentation highlights.

The model layer shows how the zoo stays manageable. model_factory.cc registers classes by config, models/transformer.cc at 153 lines handles the encoder-decoder family, language_model.cc at 406 lines covers decoder-only generation with SequenceGeneratorReplica::generate at 56 and DecoderReplica::run_generation at 150, and whisper.cc at 865 lines adds audio: encode at 80, two generate paths at 122 and 233, cross-attention alignment at 425 using dynamic time warping over dtw.cc, and detect_language at 585. Each architecture implements the same Decoder contract from decoder.cc, update_state at 33 and replicate_state at 57, which is how the KV-cache states stay architecture-agnostic. The ops layer follows the strict three-file pattern, dispatcher, _cpu.cc, _gpu.cu, seen in gemm.cc with operator() at 45, covering everything from rms_norm and rotary embeddings to conv1d with an optional cuDNN path, and nccl_ops.cc adds the collectives behind tensor parallelism for models too large for one GPU.

The integration surface completes the picture. python/cpp/translator.cc registers TranslatorWrapper at line 275 alongside generator, Whisper, wav2vec2, and MPI wrappers, while python/ctranslate2 ships the converters and a specs package whose declarative layer descriptions, transformer_spec.py, whisper_spec.py, wav2vec2_spec.py, define what the serialized format holds, the same specs the C++ classes read back. setup.py wires seven ct2 converter console scripts, and the cli folder builds the native binary over the same C++ API. The CUDA runtime is careful about its dependencies: allocator.cc at 187 lines caches device memory, and cuBLAS, NCCL, and MPI are loaded through dlopen stub files, cublas_stub.cc, nccl_stub.cc, mpi_stub.cc, so the wheel installs and runs even where vendor libraries are absent.

From Install to a Served Model

Install, convert a Hugging Face checkpoint, and run translation or generation:

pip install ctranslate2
ct2-transformers-converter --model t5-small --output_dir t5-ct2 --quantization int8

import ctranslate2

generator = ctranslate2.Generator("t5-ct2")
results = generator.generate_batch(
    [["encode the sentence", "with the encoder-decoder"]],
    max_length=32,
)
print(results[0].sequences)

The same two-step pattern serves Whisper speech models, BERT embeddings, and Llama-family generation, with the quantization flag choosing where each weight lands on the precision ladder.

Honest limits: the model zoo covers the architectures the project chose, so a novel architecture means writing a converter and a C++ model class, training is out of scope by design, and the custom format is not the ONNX exchange format, so the two ecosystems meet only through converters. The GPU attention fast paths target sm80 and newer, and int8 on GPU assumes supported hardware. None of that changes the core fact: this is one of the cleanest custom inference runtimes in open source, small enough to read completely and fast enough that production translation servers still run on it, MIT-licensed in a single compact tree.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of OpenNMT/CTranslate2: the optimized model format, the converter suite, replica pools and beam search decoding, per-device op dispatch, the int8 CPU kernel path with fused activations, vendored FlashAttention-2 and AWQ int4 on GPU, Whisper alignment, and the five-backend CPU story.

entry.title: The Template Cathedral of GEMM - Inside NVIDIA/cutlass

link.title: The Template Cathedral of GEMM - Inside NVIDIA/cutlass

entry.content:
Every training run and every inference server on NVIDIA hardware eventually bottoms out in a matrix multiply, and for most of the industry that multiply comes from CUTLASS. Started in 2017 and cited by Vijay Thakkar and colleagues, the project at version 4.8.0 in this tree is NVIDIA’s collection of C++ template abstractions for high-performance GEMM and its relatives, BSD 3-Clause licensed, spanning FP64 through TF32, FP16, BF16, both FP8 flavors, the block-scaled NVFP4, MXFP4, MXFP6, and MXFP8 families, narrow integers, and even 1-bit types across Volta, Turing, Ampere, Ada, Hopper, Blackwell, and now the new Rubin SM107 generation. Version 4 added the CuTe DSL, Python-native kernel authoring with orders-of-magnitude faster compiles, and the README’s release notes name the company it keeps: every release is tested against FlashAttention, Quack, FlashInfer, cuDNN Frontend, PyTorch main, and TensorRT-LLM main. As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

The architecture is a hierarchy of named layers, each of which can be swapped without touching the others. At the bottom, CuTe defines layouts and tensors, the algebra of shapes, strides, and swizzles. Atoms bind that algebra to actual hardware instructions. Collectives assemble atoms into mainloops and epilogues, kernels schedule tiles across persistent blocks, and a thin device adapter exposes the whole assembly as a runnable GEMM. The Python DSL mirrors the same concepts so that a kernel written in CuTe C++ and one written with the cute.jit decorator lower to comparable PTX. Reading the overview from left to right walks one GEMM from a Layout object to a scheduled tensor-core instruction.

Overview of CUTLASS: CuTe layouts and tensors feed MMA and copy atoms bound to instruction wrappers, collective builders and warp-specialized kernels consume them through async stage machinery, the GemmUniversalAdapter exposes runnable GEMMs, the CuTe DSL mirrors it all in Python, and the Operator API plus examples and profiler close the loop.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • layout.hpp is the 1971-line heart of CuTe, defining hierarchically multidimensional layouts and the composition algebra of tiling and partitioning.
  • tensor.hpp packages a layout with a data array, with the 1124-line tensor_impl.hpp doing the iterator bookkeeping.
  • The atom folder holds instruction traits such as mma_traits_sm107.hpp at 565 lines and copy_traits_sm90.hpp for TMA loads.
  • The arch folder wraps raw PTX across 35 files, led by mma_sm100_umma.hpp at 2041 lines for Blackwell’s tcgen05 instructions.
  • The kernel layer stages warp-specialized GEMMs per generation, from sm90 cooperative and pingpong variants to sm100_gemm_tma_warpspecialized.hpp at 964 lines and the Rubin sm107 kernel.
  • GemmUniversalAdapter at class line 123 of an 819-line file turns any kernel-plus-collectives assembly into a runnable device GEMM.
  • Tile schedulers at 826 lines map output tiles to persistent blocks, with group and stream-K siblings for MoE workloads and tail smoothing.
  • cute/core.py is the Python DSL heart at 6728 lines, with tile_to_shape at 5139 and local_partition at 5177.

Why You Need This

Writing a GEMM that hits hardware peak is the classic months-long systems project: shared-memory bank conflicts, register pressure, async copy staging, and instruction scheduling all interact, and every new GPU generation resets the board. CUTLASS exists so that nobody has to restart that project. Its README charts show the 3.x kernels operating at a large fraction of theoretical peak on Blackwell SM100 across every supported dtype, and because PyTorch, TensorRT-LLM, FlashAttention, and FlashInfer all build on these templates, the performance work NVIDIA ships here propagates through the entire ecosystem at the next dependency bump. If you have ever wondered where the speed of an fp8 or block-scaled fp4 matmul actually comes from, the answer is data movement planned by these headers: TMA bulk copies staged through multi-stage buffers, accumulators parked in tensor memory, and warpgroups kept busy with cooperative or pingpong overlap.

The second reason is portability of ideas. CuTe’s insight is that a kernel is mostly bookkeeping, and bookkeeping can be expressed as layout algebra: a partition, a tiling, a swizzle are values you can print, compose, and reason about without running anything. Once your mainloop is written against atoms and layouts rather than raw instructions, retargeting it is a matter of swapping the atom. That is exactly how this repository carries one conceptual design from Volta’s mma instructions through Hopper’s wgmma, Blackwell’s tcgen05 with 2-SM variants, and Rubin’s SM107 UMMA with FP8 at MMA_K=64 and FP4 at MMA_K=128, extended tensor memory of 576 columns, and 328 KB of shared memory. The compatibility table runs from a V100 on CUDA 11.4 to B300 and DGX Spark on CUDA 13.0, with the caveat that architecture-accelerated instructions require the sm_90a and sm_100a targets and that Rubin needs the R615 driver from CUDA 13.4 GA.

The third reason is the Python door. The CuTe DSL lets you write kernels with the cute.jit and cute.kernel decorators, traced into the same IR the C++ templates emit, with compile times in seconds instead of minutes and no glue code to call it from PyTorch. FlashAttention-4, which we toured earlier in this series, is written in exactly this DSL, and this release keeps polishing the path: the cute_ext extension compiler preview via CUTE_DSL_USE_EXTENSION_COMPILER=1, x86_64 Windows support, ahead-of-time host targets including QNX 8.0, JAX integration through cutlass.jax.cutlass_call, and an Operator API whose candidates can now be ranked by nvMatmulHeuristics on Blackwell. For framework authors the deal is simple: describe an operator in cutlass.operators, get a tuned kernel without writing C++.

Detail view: int_tuple and swizzle feed layout.hpp, tensor_impl glues iterators to layouts, atom traits wrap SM90 wgmma, SM100 tcgen05, and SM107 UMMA instructions, the adapter runs cooperative and warpspecialized kernels through builders and stage machinery, and the DSL and Operator API surfaces mirror the C++ stack.

The CuTe core is small enough to read in an afternoon and rewards it. int_tuple.hpp defines the hierarchical integer tuples that serve as shapes and strides, swizzle.hpp adds bit-swizzled layout wrappers that permute shared-memory addresses to dodge bank conflicts, and layout.hpp composes them into the 1971-line algebra at the center. tensor_impl.hpp, 1124 lines, glues an iterator to a layout and supplies local_tile and local_partition, the two calls every mainloop uses to slice a global problem into per-block tiles. algorithm/gemm.hpp then provides the 500-line generic MMA loop that consumes atom traits over partitioned tensors, with functional.hpp adding elementwise combinators for fused work. Print a layout with cute::print and the whole abstraction becomes concrete, which is why the tutorials lean on it so heavily.

The instruction floor shows three generations side by side. For Hopper, mma_traits_sm90.hpp, at 144 lines, declares wgmma atom traits, and copy_traits_sm90.hpp lets mainloops express TMA loads as ordinary CuTe copies. For Blackwell, mma_sm100_umma.hpp spans 2041 lines of tcgen05 UMMA wrappers with its 957-line descriptor builder in mma_sm100_desc.hpp encoding dtype, transpose, and scale-mode bitfields. For Rubin, mma_sm107_umma.hpp, 553 lines, pairs with mma_traits_sm107.hpp at 565 lines. Above them, the kernel layer files are named like a menu: sm90_gemm_tma_warpspecialized_cooperative.hpp runs 893 lines with a pingpong sibling that overlaps epilogues, sm100_gemm_tma_warpspecialized.hpp runs 964 lines parking accumulators in tensor memory, and sm107_gemm_tma_warpspecialized.hpp reuses the SM100 builder family against Rubin’s larger memories. The collective builders do the assembly, sm100_umma_builder.inl at 350 lines for mainloops and the 1841-line sm100 epilogue builder for TMEM epilogues with fusion callbacks, while the 1406-line Hopper stage-machinery header choreographs TMA barriers between producer and consumer warps.

The adapter and its predecessors complete the C++ story. GemmUniversalAdapter, defined at line 123 of gemm_universal_adapter.h, initializes workspace, picks occupancy-aware launch parameters, and runs any assembled kernel behind one interface, which is why a single example file can swap schedules without changing call sites. The 2.x world still lives beside it: default_gemm_universal.h and its siblings cover sparse, grouped, rank-2K, planar-complex, and split-K assemblies from the Volta and Ampere era, all resting on the warp-level mma.h at 90 lines. Tile scheduling matured alongside, from the sm90 scheduler with group and stream-K variants to the 826-line sm100 scheduler with cluster-aware and dynamic persistent modes that Blackwell MoE kernels lean on.

The Python stack mirrors all of it. cute/core.py, at 6728 lines, re-exports the layout algebra with tile_to_shape at 5139 and local_partition at 5177, tensor.py adds a 3309-line Tensor whose copy and partition calls lower to the same paths as C++, and cutlass_dsl/cutlass.py hosts the decorators users actually write, jit at 1878 and kernel at 1957, traced by the pyir engine under base_dsl. The working example is in the repo: examples/python/CuTeDSL/dsl_tutorials/call_from_jit.py imports cutlass and cutlass.cute, wraps a GEMM in an @cute.jit function at line 163, and converts PyTorch buffers through the JitArgument protocol. The Operator API sits a level higher in operators/cutlass/operators with base.py describing intent and manifest.py enumerating candidates, and operators/cutlass/kernels exposes standalone persistent GEMMs including a Rubin flavor, callable without any operator ceremony. The 100 example directories, from 88_hopper_fmha through 92_blackwell_moe_gemm and 93_blackwell_low_latency_gqa to the cute/rubin block-scaled samples, double as the test corpus for the profiler under tools.

From Install to a Tuned GEMM

Build from source with the architecture-specific flags, then sweep configurations with the bundled profiler:

git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass.git
cd cutlass && mkdir build && cd build
cmake .. -DCUTLASS_NVCC_ARCHS="90a;100a" -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
make cutlass_profiler -j
./tools/profiler/cutlass_profiler --operation=GEMM --m=4096 --n=4096 --k=4096

For the Python DSL, install the wheel and trace a kernel with the same decorators the repo’s tutorials use:

import cutlass
import cutlass.cute as cute

@cute.jit
def tensor_op_gemm_wrapper(a_tma, b_tma, mC, mD, ...):
    # compose layouts, partition tiles, launch the kernel
    ...

# examples/python/CuTeDSL/dsl_tutorials/call_from_jit.py shows the full flow:
# PyTorch tensors enter through make_ptr, exit as a JIT-compiled GEMM result

pip install nvidia-cutlass-dsl gives you the DSL package that FlashAttention-4 and the Operator API build on, and the notebooks under examples/python/CuTeDSL/cute/notebooks walk from first layout to block-scaled GEMM.

Honest limits: this is template metaprogramming, and C++ compile times for instantiated kernels remain a real tax, which is precisely why the DSL exists. Windows builds for the 3.x C++ stack are currently broken per the README, the sm_90a and sm_100a targets trade forward compatibility for speed, and GeForce RTX 50 owners on SM120 cannot run SM100 datacenter kernels. The Operator API is young and its Rubin support is explicitly a preview pending performance tuning. None of that changes the core fact: if a matrix multiply matters to your workload, the most battle-tested implementations on the planet are open source in this single tree.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of NVIDIA/cutlass: how CuTe layouts and tensors compose into MMA atoms, the warp-specialized SM90, SM100, and SM107 kernel layer, the GemmUniversalAdapter, the Python CuTe DSL compiler, and the Operator API that frameworks call.
