entry.title: The Vector Search Engine Under the Databases - Inside rapidsai/cuvs

link.title: The Vector Search Engine Under the Databases - Inside rapidsai/cuvs

entry.content:
Every retrieval-augmented generation stack, every recommendation feed, and every semantic search box eventually asks the same question: given this vector, which of the hundred million stored vectors are its nearest neighbors? Apache-2.0 licensed cuVS, version 26.12.00 on the RAPIDS release train, is NVIDIA’s answer, and it is the layer that an increasing number of databases call rather than reimplement. The README describes it as state-of-the-art implementations of approximate nearest neighbors and clustering on the GPU, built on top of the RAPIDS RAFT primitives, usable directly or through the libraries that have integrated it. What makes the tree special is the coverage: one C ABI, four idiomatic language APIs, a dozen index types from exact brute force to learned quantization, and a build-on-GPU, deploy-on-CPU story for the edge. As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

The headline algorithm is CAGRA, a GPU-native graph index published in a 2023 paper whose build and search the repository implements end to end. Around it sit the IVF family in four quantization regimes, graph builders like NN-Descent and Vamana, a 3015-line CPU HNSW engine, clustering that includes the cuSLINK single-linkage paper implementation, and a top-k selection stack strong enough that its own research paper is cited in the README. The tree is organized for portability: cpp/include/cuvs holds the public headers, cpp/src the CUDA kernels, c/include the stable C surface, and python, rust, go, and java folders each carry a native-feeling API. Reading the overview from left to right walks one query from a language binding down through graph traversal kernels to a ranked result list.

Overview of cuVS: graph builders and the CAGRA index define the searchable structures, CUDA detail kernels implement build and search, the IVF family trains its lists through the clustering suite, brute force feeds the top-k selection machinery, and one C ABI carries everything to Python, Rust, Go, and Java, with HNSW bridging GPU indexes to CPU deployment and multi-GPU sharding on top.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • cagra.hpp is the flagship at 4979 lines: search_params at 56, ace_params at 173 for partitioned builds that exceed GPU memory, the index class at 486, and merge_params at 3474.
  • ivf_flat.hpp at 3579 lines is the inverted-file workhorse, with index_params at 28, list_spec at 87, and the index at 137.
  • ivf_rabitq.hpp compresses vectors to 1 through 9 bits per dimension, defaulting to 3 at line 54, with a search_mode enum at 95 offering LUT16, LUT32, QUANT4, and QUANT8 scan modes.
  • brute_force.hpp at 952 lines is the exact baseline that papers benchmark against, alongside scann.hpp at 408 lines for the two-level ScaNN design.
  • nn_descent.hpp at 623 lines and vamana.hpp at 664 build the k-NN graphs that CAGRA consumes, while tiered_index.hpp at 273 wraps any index for incremental inserts.
  • cagra_build.cuh is the 1250-line kernel layer behind the build, with build_knn_graph at 156 and host-side refinement at 110.
  • select_k.hpp at 203 lines is the public face of the top-k machinery from the Top-K on GPU paper, shared by every index in the tree.
  • cagra.h is the stable C surface: cuvsCagraBuild at 710, cuvsCagraSearch at 804, SerializeToHnswlib at 922, and Merge at 1079, all over DLPack tensors.

Why You Need This

The first reason is the throughput story at database scale. Vector search at a hundred million rows is memory-bound, and the difference between a good index and a great one is how few random reads each query needs. CAGRA’s answer is a graph built specifically for GPU warp-level traversal, and the repository lets you watch the whole construction: build_knn_graph in cagra_build.cuh computes the intermediate neighborhood, graph_core.cuh prunes it to the final degree, and cagra_ace.cuh implements Augmented Core Extraction, the partitioned build that streams clusters through GPU memory when the dataset will not fit. Search runs as multiple coordinated kernels in the 713-line search_multi_kernel.cuh, scoring candidates through compute_distance templates generated for raw and vector-quantized datasets. If you run Milvus, Vespa, or any engine that has integrated cuVS, this is the code your latency is made of.

The second reason is the quantization ladder, which pairs beautifully with the weight quantization we toured in the torchao post. The IVF family spans four regimes: ivf_flat keeps full-precision vectors per inverted list, ivf_pq.hpp at 3451 lines interleaves product-quantized codes for memory-constrained serving, ivf_sq scalar-quantizes per dimension, and ivf_rabitq.hpp implements the GPU-native RaBitQ design with 1 to 9 bits per dimension, kmeans-trained coarse centroids, and lookup-table search modes. RaBitQ’s header even documents streaming construction with streaming_batch_size at line 70 and force_streaming at 84, so an index larger than device memory builds straight from host storage. Understanding when each regime wins is exactly the recall-versus-memory tradeoff that vector database architects are paid to navigate, and here every knob is documented in the same header that implements it.

The third reason is the portability discipline. One C ABI in c/include speaks DLPack, which means tensors arrive from PyTorch, CuPy, or your own buffer format without copies, and the four language bindings all sit on that ABI: Cython modules like cagra.pyx for Python, a cuvs-sys FFI crate for Rust with index.rs exposing build, search, search_filtered, and serialize_to_hnswlib, Go packages per index over dlpack.go, and Java through JDK 22 Panama bindings. The Java folder also ships cuvs-lucene, a pluggable Lucene KnnVectorsFormat that offloads vector indexing to the GPU through a codec, so an existing Lucene or Elasticsearch stack accelerates with minimal code changes. And the SerializeToHnswlib entry at line 922 of cagra.h closes the edge case: an index built on a GPU can be exported to hnswlib format and served by the 3015-line CPU HNSW engine in detail/hnsw.hpp.

Detail view: cagra.hpp drives build and search entries into the CUDA detail kernels, ivf_common.cuh backs the flat, PQ, RaBitQ, and SQ variants with kmeans-trained codebooks, the top-k and bitonic machinery ranks candidates, HNSW and multi-GPU layers extend deployment, and the binding stack from DLPack to Lucene carries it all to users.

The CAGRA internals repay a slow read. The public header declares a variant of graph builders at line 253, so the same index can be built with ivf_pq_params, nn_descent_params, or ace_params depending on dataset size, and search_params at 56 add iterative search for oversized candidate sets. In the detail folder, cagra_build.cuh chains build_knn_graph at 156 through write_to_graph at 86 and refine_host_and_write_graph at 110, while the search side pairs cagra_search.cuh with compute_distance templates instantiated per dtype from matrix.json manifests, the same JIT-style instantiation trick that keeps compile times sane across fp32, fp16, int8, and uint8. The topk_for_cagra folder with its topk.cu and topk_core.cuh implements the radix-style candidate pruning, bitonic.hpp sorts partial result lists, and cagra_merge.cuh combines indexes grown independently, which is also what the C API’s Merge entry at 1079 exposes to databases doing continuous ingestion.

The IVF family shows how much machinery one shared abstraction absorbs. ivf_common.cuh and ivf_list.cuh define the inverted-list layout every variant reuses, and the differences are all in what a list stores: full vectors for flat, interleaved PQ codes with the list_spec_interleaved struct at line 235 of ivf_pq.hpp, per-dimension scalars for SQ, or the low-bit RaBitQ codes with their LUT scan modes. Codebooks come from kmeans.hpp at 1897 lines, with balanced_kmeans_example.cu demonstrating the size-evening variant that keeps GPU lists uniform. Filters integrate at the same layer: roaring_bitmap_filter.cu and sample_filter.cu let a search exclude masked rows, the examples folder shows both a roaring bitmap and a Bloom filter variant, and the Python filters.pyx wraps them for user code. Reachability and sparse k-NN kernels under detail round out the graph-analysis use cases the README lists for UMAP and cuGraph integration.

The binding and deployment stack is the quiet engineering triumph. Python’s cagra.pyx at 1161 lines mirrors the C++ surface with build at 453, search at 823, and extend at 1112, over cydlpack.pyx conversions and resources.pyx stream handling, with mg_resources.pyx and the mg packages exposing single-node multi-GPU built on snmg.cuh. The C API even provides IndexParamsFromHnswParams at line 328, acknowledging the migration path from existing hnswlib deployments. Rust’s index.rs exposes search_filtered at 154 and hnswlib export at 215, Go ships per-index packages with a shared distance.go metric zoo, and the Java side documents its filter bitset device pool down to the RMM 4 MiB initial reservation. Distance itself lives in the 471-line distance.hpp behind pairwise_distance at line 51 of distance.pyx, the same metric set every index consumes.

From Install to a Searched Index

Install the Python package, build a CAGRA index, and search it, exactly as the README shows:

pip install cuvs-cu12
# or: conda install -c rapidsai -c conda-forge -c nvidia cuvs

import cupy as cp
from cuvs.neighbors import cagra

dataset = cp.random.random((100000, 64), dtype=cp.float32)

index_params = cagra.IndexParams(
    intermediate_graph_degree=128, graph_degree=64
)
index = cagra.build(index_params, dataset)

queries = cp.random.random((10, 64), dtype=cp.float32)
search_params = cagra.SearchParams(itopk_size=32)
neighbors, distances = cagra.search(search_params, index, queries, 10)

The same CAGRA flow reads almost identically in C, Rust, and Go, because every binding implements the same lifecycle of params, build, search, and destroy over DLPack tensors.

Honest limits: cuVS is GPU-first, so the Python API expects CUDA arrays and the prebuilt wheels are tied to specific CUDA major versions, with the README noting the CUDA 13 builds are roughly half the binary size of CUDA 12 builds. Exact recall reproduction against research numbers takes parameter work, the Java API is flagged experimental in its own README, and the ACE partitioned build trades build time for memory headroom. None of that changes the core fact: the fastest open vector search kernels on NVIDIA hardware, plus the CPU fallback and the multi-language surface, live in this one Apache-2.0 tree, and reading them will make every downstream vector database make sense.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of rapidsai/cuvs: the CAGRA graph index with its Augmented Core Extraction builds, the IVF family from flat lists to nine-bit RaBitQ codebooks, brute force and ScaNN, GPU graph builders, the top-k selection machinery, HNSW for CPU deployment, and one C ABI behind Python, Rust, Go, Java, and Lucene.

entry.title: The Library That Indexes Billions - Inside facebookresearch/faiss

link.title: The Library That Indexes Billions - Inside facebookresearch/faiss

entry.content:
Every recommendation feed, duplicate detector, and retrieval-augmented answer starts with the same question: of these billion vectors, which few are closest to mine? Faiss, started by Herve Jegou at Meta’s Fundamental AI Research group and maintained by an author list that reads like a history of the field, has been the standard answer since 2017. The MIT-licensed C++ library, now at version 1.15.1 with 207 cpp files and 286 headers under faiss/ alone, implements exact search, inverted files, graph indexes, and a shelf of quantizer codecs, wraps all of it through SWIG for Python with typed stubs, exposes a stable C API, and ports the hot paths to CUDA with 75.cu files plus an Apple Metal variant. Its research lineage is documented in three citable papers, from the 2024 overview The Faiss Library to the GPU work in Billion-scale similarity search with GPUs. As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

The design is a study in one abstraction done thoroughly. Everything is an Index: a base struct that promises train, add, and search, with distances defined as either L2 or inner product, cosine included by normalizing first. Around that contract grows a family tree, some members exact baselines, some compressed-domain codecs that never store the original vectors, some graph structures that trade memory for hops, and wrappers like IndexShards, IndexReplicas, and IndexRefine that compose any index into a distributed or re-ranking layout. A string parser named index_factory turns recipes like IVF4096,PQ32 into configured objects, which is why every tutorial you have ever read looks the same. Underneath, kernels do the arithmetic, with a BLAS threshold deciding when matrix multiplication beats loops, and SIMD dispatch choosing instruction sets at runtime. Reading the overview from left to right follows one recipe string to computed neighbors.

Overview of Faiss: the factory parses recipe strings into the Index contract, flat, IVF, and HNSW families provide search structures, quantizers and inverted lists handle storage, exact kernels and k-means do the math, and GPU plus Python layers carry it to hardware and users.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The Index contract is line 101 of a 430-line header: train at 132, add at 164, search, and search parameters.
  • index_factory at line 1258 of 1330 lines parses recipe strings, with coarse quantizer parsing at 285.
  • IndexFlat is the exact baseline at line 21, with IP at 87, L2 at 92, and a Panorama layout at 114.
  • IndexIVF spans 1784 lines: search_preassigned at 495, add_core at 306.
  • IndexHNSW is 1469 lines of graph search, with the graph itself in impl/HNSW.cpp at 2056 lines.
  • The quantizers run 941 lines for PQ, 714 for scalar, 795 for the 1-bit RaBitQ.
  • Inverted lists hold the data in 1003 lines, with on-disk and blocked variants beside them.
  • The GPU layer clones any CPU index to CUDA in 617 lines of to_gpu and to_cpu logic.

Why You Need This

The first reason is that the index zoo is not a pile of classes, it is a composition system, and reading it teaches you how search systems are actually layered. An IndexIVF needs a coarse quantizer, which is itself an Index; an IndexHNSW can store raw floats, PQ codes, or RaBitQ codes through constructor choices; IndexPreTransform wraps any index with a PCA or OPQ rotation; IndexRefine re-ranks another index’s output with full-precision rescoring; IndexShards and IndexReplicas spread one dataset across machines or GPUs. The factory string grammar mirrors this: IVF4096,PQ32 means cluster into 4096 cells, encode members with 32 sub-quantizers, and the 1330-line parser maps every token to a constructor call. Once you see the pattern, the 40-plus index types stop being trivia and become a menu of trade-offs along search time, quality, memory, and build cost that the README tabulates explicitly.

The second reason is the performance engineering, which is meticulous at every scale. The exact kernels in a 1405-line distances.cpp switch between plain loops and BLAS matrix multiplication based on a documented threshold of 128000 floating operations, tile the computation to cache, and specialize fp16 and Top1 variants; the SIMD layer dispatches between instruction sets at runtime, with the changelog recording the addition of dynamic AVX512 popcount levels. The IVF scanners and quantizer decoders are hand-tuned, the HNSW implementation tracks per-visit tables to avoid re-scanning, and the GPU port covers flat, IVF, IVFPQ, IVF scalar quantizer, binary flat, and Cagra graph search, with cuVS available as an optional backend. Even serialization has zerocopy and memory-mapped readers, because at billion scale the cost of loading an index rivals the cost of searching it.

The third reason is trust: this is one of the few numerical libraries where the reference implementations ship next to the fast ones on purpose. Every quantizer has a slow, obvious decoder you can diff against; distances.cpp keeps exhaustive sequence kernels beside the tiled BLAS ones; the clustering module’s kmeans_clustering function at line 526 is a forty-year-old algorithm in modern clothing with subsampling, GPU offload, and a SuperKMeans extension visible in the Python wrappers. The tutorial directory carries parallel cpp and python versions of the same examples, the C API gives non-C++ languages a stable 49-file surface, and the doxygen site documents every class. When your production search starts returning strange results, this is the codebase you can actually debug down to the kernel.

The detailed map: the API and wrapper layer, flat and IVF structures, graph indexes, the quantizer shelf, compute and storage layers, and the GPU plus binding stacks.

Follow one recipe through the factory first. The Index struct at line 101 declares the contract: train on a sample, add vectors one batch at a time, search with k results, and optionally respect SearchParameters structs that tune recall per call, defined at line 88. The factory splits the string on commas and dispatches to parse functions, from parse_coarse_quantizer at 285 to the newer parse_svs_datatype at 692 that wires in the third-party SVS backend, whose Flat, IVF, and Vamana variants with LeanVec and LVQ compression live under faiss/svs. Composition wrappers keep the grammar open-ended: VectorTransform.cpp at 1643 lines supplies the PCA and OPQ matrices that IndexPreTransform applies transparently, IndexRefine at 397 lines holds a base index plus full vectors for re-ranking, and IndexShards at 271 lines fans a query out to sub-indexes.

The two workhorse families deserve separate reads. IndexIVF clusters the dataset with k-means from Clustering.cpp, whose train function at line 48 and train_impl at 92 handle subsampling and numeric types, then stores each vector’s code in the inverted lists of 1003 lines, an abstract array interface whose on-disk variant spills to files and whose blocked variant batches allocation; a DirectMap, enabled at line 383, turns remove calls from scans into lookups. At query time, search_preassigned at line 495 probes nprobe lists, and a per-list InvertedListScanner, declared at line 543 of IndexIVF.h, accumulates distances, which is how IVFPQ, IVFSQ, and IVFRaBitQ all reuse one search driver. IndexHNSW takes the graph route: search at 509 walks the layered graph, add at 559 inserts with the greedy descent in impl/HNSW.cpp, 2056 lines that include add_links_starting_from at 635 and the candidate search at 1117, while NSG and NNDescent in the same impl directory provide alternative graph builds and IndexHNSWCagra at line 261 imports GPU-built Cagra graphs for CPU search.

The quantizer shelf is where memory per vector drops from 1024 bytes to a handful. ProductQuantizer at 941 lines splits each vector into sub-vectors, codes each against a learned codebook, and provides generic, 8-bit, and 16-bit encoder and decoder structs; ScalarQuantizer at 714 lines quantizes per-dimension ranges into 8 or fewer bits; RaBitQuantizer at 795 lines encodes each vector as a single bit per dimension plus error bounds, with a multi-bit variant and a dedicated code packer in impl. The additive family, residual and local search quantizers with their training utilities, composes multiple codebooks, and the polysemous training plus lattice modules refine the codes for hamming-distance search. All of them feed the SIMD dispatch for fast decode, and the Panorama layout, exposed as IndexFlatPanorama at line 114 of IndexFlat.h, shows the newest idea in the tree, pruning distance computations using sorted attribute order.

The compute and porting layers complete the story. distances.cpp implements every exact kernel, from exhaustive_inner_product_seq at 286 to the BLAS tiled path at 545, gated by the threshold constant at line 705 and pushing results into the ResultHandler sinks from impl. Serialization lives in index_read.cpp, 3728 lines that deserialize every index type ever shipped, with a 1452-line writer and four IO flavors including memory mapping. The GPU side starts from GpuCloner.cpp, whose to_gpu function turns any CPU index into a GpuIndex, backed by GpuIndexFlat, GpuIndexIVFFlat at 393 lines, GpuIndexIVFPQ at 622, and the CUDA brute-force kernels of GpuDistance, all prefixed by a GpuClonerOptions struct that tunes temporary memory and allocation, with GpuAutoTune searching those options. Bindings close the loop: the SWIG interface at 1460 lines generates the Python module that init.py assembles with 605 lines of helpers, class_wrappers.py adds 1680 lines of argument validation and clustering wrappers, py.typed and the stub file give IDEs real signatures, and the 49-file C API at the top level mirrors every index for languages without SWIG.

From Install to a Search

Conda packages are the supported path, with pip wheels and source builds documented in INSTALL.md:

conda install -c pytorch faiss-cpu
# GPU build:
conda install -c pytorch faiss-gpu

Then the canonical four-line tour, straight from the library’s own conventions:

import numpy as np
import faiss

d = 64
nb, nq = 100000, 10000
xb = np.random.random((nb, d)).astype("float32")
xq = np.random.random((nq, d)).astype("float32")

index = faiss.IndexFlatL2(d)
index.add(xb)
D, I = index.search(xq, 5)

The factory is the real entry point: faiss.index_factory(64, “IVF4096,PQ32”) builds the two-level index, but it needs training first, so call index.train on a representative sample of at least about 39 times 4096 vectors per the library’s own rule of thumb, then add, then search. Swap the recipe for “IVF4096,HNSW32” or “OPQ32_64,IVF4096,PQ32” and the same four calls run a different point on the speed-quality-memory curve, and faiss.extract_index_ivf or the GpuCloner functions let you reach in and reconfigure or move it to the GPU without changing the search code.

Honest limits: the GPU build is Linux and Windows only through conda, not macOS, where the Metal port covers a subset of index types; IVF indexes with many vectors per list can bottleneck on single-threaded list scanning unless the NUMA and threading guides in the wiki are followed; the factory grammar is powerful but unforgiving, and an invalid recipe errors out only at parse time; and the C API, while broad, lags new index types by design so its surface stays stable. Start with the Index header, then the factory, then one index family end to end; that order turns a dense catalog into a system you can extend.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of facebookresearch/faiss: how the Index contract, the index factory recipe parser, IVF and HNSW structures, quantizer codecs, handwritten CUDA kernels, and SWIG bindings fit together into Meta's similarity search library.

entry.title: The Kernel That Rewrote Attention - Inside Dao-AILab/flash-attention

link.title: The Kernel That Rewrote Attention - Inside Dao-AILab/flash-attention

entry.content:
Every transformer trained since 2022 owes part of its existence to a paper proof that attention could be computed without ever writing the full sequence-by-sequence matrix to HBM. FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness by Tri Dao, Daniel Y. Fu, Stefano Ermon, Atri Rudra, and Christopher Re appeared at NeurIPS 2022, and its successor FlashAttention-2, a single-author work Tri Dao presented at ICLR 2024, became the de facto attention kernel for the industry. The BSD 3-Clause licensed repository that carries both is one of those rare codebases where a systems insight, memory traffic dominates math, is visible in every directory: a Python front end that never allocates what it can fuse, a C++ binding layer that dispatches on head dimension, and three kernel generations for three GPU eras. As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

The repository is organized as an archaeology of GPU hardware. The main package implements FlashAttention-2 for Ampere, Ada, and Hopper GPUs with a generated grid of CUDA files. The hopper folder is a beta FlashAttention-3 that rewrites the mainloop around TMA copies, warp specialization, and Hopper’s GMMA tensor core instructions. The flash_attn.cute package is FlashAttention-4, a CuTeDSL implementation for Hopper and Blackwell that expresses the whole algorithm in Python-embedded tile primitives. Around them sit a fused GPT reference model, optimized rotary and norm layers, a training folder for GPT2 and GPT3, and a ROCm port with two AMD backends. Reading the overview from left to right follows one attention call from the Python signature down to a specific compiled kernel file.

Overview of FlashAttention: the flash_attn Python API binds to the C++ mha_fwd entry, which launches the generated SM80 kernel grid; MHA modules and the GPT reference model sit on top, while FA3, FA4, the ROCm CK backend, the Triton variant, and the test suite surround them.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • flash_attn_interface.py is the public surface, 1629 lines with flash_attn_func at 1156, flash_attn_qkvpacked_func at 1019, flash_attn_varlen_func at 1391, and flash_attn_with_kvcache at 1485.
  • flash_api.cpp is the C++ binding at 1538 lines, opening with mha_fwd at line 370.
  • The SM80 kernel grid holds 116 files enumerating head dims, dtypes, causal flags, and split-KV variants.
  • mha.py is the module layer at 993 lines, with the full projection-carrying MHA at line 373.
  • models/gpt.py builds a complete GPT at 1080 lines, GPTLMHeadModel at 577.
  • hopper/flash_attn_interface.py is FlashAttention-3 at 1146 lines, flash_attn_func at 809.
  • cute/interface.py is FlashAttention-4, 4970 lines with flash_attn_func at 4145.
  • tests/test_flash_attn.py enforces the project’s correctness bar: max numerical error at most twice a PyTorch reference.

Why You Need This

Standard attention materializes an N-by-N score matrix in GPU memory, so a 32-thousand-token sequence in bfloat16 would need gigabytes before the softmax even starts. FlashAttention computes exact attention in linear memory by tiling: load K and V blocks, maintain running max and sum statistics, rescale as you go. The README’s memory chart shows 10x savings at 2K tokens and 20x at 4K, which is what unlocked long-context training before anyone sold you a sparse approximation. Because the result is exact, every downstream user from Mistral’s sliding-window models to Gemma-2’s softcapping could adopt it without changing their math, and the changelog reads like a history of transformer research: variable-length batches in 2.0, bottom-right causal alignment in 2.1, split-KV decode in 2.2 contributed with the xformers team’s Daniel Haziza, sliding windows in 2.3 with Mistral AI, ALiBi in 2.4 thanks to Sanghun Cho at Kakao Brain, deterministic backward from Meituan engineers, paged KV cache in 2.5 matching the PagedAttention paper, softcapping in 2.6 from HuggingFace’s Narsil and lucidrains, and torch.compile compatibility in 2.7.

The decode side is where serving lives or dies. flash_attn_with_kvcache accepts a pre-allocated key and value cache with cache_seqlens, updates it in place with new tokens, applies rotary embedding inside the same kernel, and supports paged caches through a block_table where each page must be a multiple of 256 elements, the exact shape of work vLLM-style servers produce. When the query length is one, the kernel splits cache loading across thread blocks and combines partial results, a collaboration with the xformers team that turned single-token generation into a bandwidth-bound rather than latency-bound problem. Grouped-query attention is handled by letting K and V carry fewer heads than Q as long as the counts divide evenly, so Llama-class models need no special mode.

The training story is just as concrete. The repository ships a full GPT implementation plus fused MLP, LayerNorm, cross-entropy, and rotary layers, and its training folder measures 3-5x speedup over the HuggingFace baseline, reaching up to 225 TFLOPs per second per A100, equivalent to 72 percent model FLOPs utilization, without activation checkpointing. FA3 pushes Hopper hardware further with FP8 forward support, and FA4 extends to Blackwell. Adoption is catalogued in the repo’s usage.md, and if compiling is too heavy, the HuggingFace kernels library serves prebuilt wheels: get_kernel(“kernels-community/flash-attn2”) returns a ready flash_attn_func.

Detail view: the Python API wraps autograd functions and flattening utilities, the C++ entry dispatches into trait-templated SM80 kernels generated by script, FA3 pairs a warp-specialized mainloop with 451 instantiations, FA4 splits forward, backward, and MLA kernels in CuTeDSL, and modules, model, ops, and training consume the API.

The Python layer is thin by design. The autograd classes FlashAttnQKVPackedFunc at line 461 and FlashAttnFunc at 828 store the output’s log-sum-exp statistics and the dropout RNG state, then recompute nothing during backward except through the C++ kernel. bert_padding.py, 218 lines, provides unpad_input and pad_input, the flattening step that turns a padded batch into packed total-token arrays so the varlen entry points never waste threads on padding. The packed variants exist because stacking Q, K, V into one tensor lets backward skip three separate gradient concatenations, a small API decision with measurable throughput value. flash_attn_with_kvcache at 1485 rounds out the set, refusing a backward pass since decode never needs one.

The C++ middle layer does shape policing and kernel selection. flash_api.cpp validates strides and head dims, then calls mha_fwd at 370, mha_varlen_fwd at 540, mha_bwd at 802, mha_varlen_bwd at 1012, and mha_fwd_kvcache at 1245. Below it, the src folder’s 116 files are enumerations: for each head dimension in 32, 64, 96, 128, 192, 256, for fp16 and bf16, causal or not, plain or split, a generated .cu file instantiates the templates in kernel_traits.h, which fix tile sizes and shared-memory staging per combination. The actual math lives in flash_fwd_kernel.h, an online-softmax loop over K and V tiles, flash_bwd_kernel.h, which recompute-then-accumulate gradients using the saved LSE, and softmax.h, the running-state struct both share. generate_kernels.py writes the instantiation files so the compiler never has to chew a monolithic template, a build-time trick mirrored in the Hopper folder.

The third and fourth generations justify their own directories. FA3’s mainloop_fwd_sm90_tma_gmma_ws.hpp name says it all: TMA asynchronous copies feed a warp-specialized stage machine where producer warps load tiles and consumer warps run GMMA tensor-core instructions, with epilogue_fwd.hpp handling final rescaling and tile_scheduler.hpp assigning work, including a persistent scheduler for variable-length batches; 451 files in hopper/instantiations cover the dtype, head-dim, and packing matrix. FA4 replaces C++ with CuTeDSL, the Python-embedded tile language from CUTLASS: interface.py at 4970 lines dispatches to flash_fwd.py and flash_bwd.py, Blackwell paths in flash_fwd_sm100.py use tcgen05 MMA with two-CTA backward variants for head dim 256, and flash_fwd_mla_sm100.py implements multi-head latent attention decode for DeepSeek-style compressed caches, with softmax.py reimplementing the running-max trick in tile form.

The model layer shows how the kernel composes into a real training stack. mha.py’s MHA at 373 carries QKV and output projections, ParallelMHA at 707 adds tensor-parallel versions, and block.py, 397 lines, wires attention, MLP, and norms into a residual block. models/gpt.py assembles everything: create_mixer_cls at 62, create_block at 262, GPTModel at 409, GPTLMHeadModel at 577, with shard_state_dict_tp at 698, a HuggingFace GPT2 weight remap at 930, and a Megatron remap at 987. The ops package supplies fused_dense.py at 688 lines, layer_norm.py at 800, rms_norm.py at 174, and layers/rotary.py at 482, each backed by its own small CUDA extension under csrc. The AMD port lives in csrc/flash_attn_ck, the Composable Kernel backend supporting MI200 through MI355X and RDNA 3/4, while the Triton backend rides in through the aiter submodule controlled by the FLASH_ATTENTION_TRITON_AMD_ENABLE flag, with an autotuning switch and a config override environment variable for tuning individual launches.

From Install to Causal Attention

Install the stable FlashAttention-2 wheel; ninja is required, since without it compilation takes around two hours on a single core versus 3-5 minutes on a 64-core machine, and MAX_JOBS caps parallelism on smaller RAM machines:

pip install flash-attn --no-build-isolation
# small-RAM machines
MAX_JOBS=4 pip install flash-attn --no-build-isolation

Run exact, causal attention with sliding window and grouped-query heads, then decode against a paged KV cache:

import torch
from flash_attn import flash_attn_func, flash_attn_with_kvcache

q = torch.randn(1, 2048, 32, 128, dtype=torch.float16, device="cuda")
k, v = torch.randn(2, 1, 2048, 8, 128, dtype=torch.float16, device="cuda")
out = flash_attn_func(q, k, v, causal=True, window_size=(1023, 0))

# incremental decoding: cache updated in place, rotary applied inside
cache_seqlens = torch.tensor([1024], dtype=torch.int32, device="cuda")
out = flash_attn_with_kvcache(q[:, -1:], k_cache, v_cache,
    cache_seqlens=cache_seqlens, causal=True)

For Hopper FP8-era performance, install the beta package from the hopper subdirectory and import flash_attn_3.flash_attn_interface; for Blackwell and beyond, pip install flash-attn-4 and import flash_attn.cute.

Honest limits: compilation is a genuine cost, Linux is the only well-tested platform, and the SM80 kernels require Ampere or newer, leaving Turing owners to a community fork. Head dims above 256 are unsupported, dropout determinism trades speed for reproducibility, and FA3 remains a separately installed beta while FA4’s CuTeDSL stack is young enough that its API surface may still move. The varlen path expects pre-flattened inputs, so integrating with padded batches means adopting the unpad and pad helpers rather than dropping in a replacement for torch’s attention call. But for what it promises, exact attention at bandwidth speed, the repository remains the reference point the entire ecosystem measures against.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of Dao-AILab/flash-attention: how the flash_attn Python API binds to the mha_fwd C++ entry, the generated SM80 kernel grid, the TMA warp-specialized Hopper FA3 stack, the CuTeDSL FA4 rewrite, and the fused GPT reference model.
